For thirty years, everyone had assumed the knocking came from loose shutters.

Then, on a windless Tuesday, it knocked back.

Mara stood at the gate with a council notice in her hand. DEMOLITION, it said, and beneath that, FRIDAY. She had come to photograph the property before the bulldozers arrived.

She tapped the gate twice with her pen.

From inside the house came two precise knocks.

Mara tapped three times.

Three knocks answered.

She ought to have called someone. Later, this would seem like the last sensible thing she could have done.

Instead, she pushed the gate.

The front door opened before she touched it.

Inside, the house smelled of rain on warm pavement. Hundreds of keys hung from the ceiling on red threads. Beneath them stood a small boy wearing a coat too large for him.

“You’re early,” he said.

“For what?”

He considered her council badge.

“Oh,” he said. “For that.”

He led her down a corridor that was much longer than the house should have allowed. Doors lined both sides. Behind one, someone laughed. Behind another came the steady scrape of a chair being dragged across a floor.

“What is this place?”

“Things people didn’t do.”

Mara stopped.

The boy opened a door.

Inside was her childhood kitchen. Yellow cupboards. A chipped blue bowl. Her father stood at the sink, his sleeves rolled up.

She caught the doorframe.

Her father had been dead twenty-three years.

In the kitchen, fourteen-year-old Mara hovered by the table, scowling.

“I hate you,” the girl said.

Her father’s shoulders tightened.

Mara remembered. The party. His refusal. The slammed door.

The heart attack before morning.

But the girl in the room didn’t leave. She hesitated, then crossed the kitchen and put her arms around him.

The boy closed the door.

“No,” Mara whispered. “Open it.”

“It isn’t what happened.”

“I know.”

“That makes it worse, usually.”

She pressed her forehead to the wood. On the other side, her father said something too quietly to hear.

After a while, she asked, “Can I go in?”

“Yes.”

“And come back?”

The boy looked down.

Above them, one of the hanging keys struck another. A tiny, bright sound.

“Who are you?” she asked.

He pulled his coat sleeves over his hands.

“There was a woman who meant to turn around at a railway station. She thought she heard someone calling her. If she’d turned, she would have missed her train.”

“And?”

“She would have met my father.”

Mara looked at the doors stretching into the dimness.

“What happens on Friday?”

“I don’t know.”

For the first time, he sounded like a child.

Mara took out her phone. No signal. She walked back toward the entrance, past a room where a bride sat alone, past another where an old man was learning to read.

At her father’s door, she stopped.

She could stay. Somewhere beyond that wood, a kettle was boiling. He would reach into the cupboard for two cups.

“Will it still be here tomorrow?” she asked.

“I think so.”

She made herself keep walking.

Outside, she called the council’s structural engineer.

“I need you to inspect something,” she said.

“What?”

She looked up. Through an upstairs window, the boy watched her.

“The interior dimensions don’t match the plans.”

By Thursday, six surveyors, two architects, and a deeply unhappy insurance assessor had entered the house.

By Thursday afternoon, demolition had been suspended indefinitely.

Mara returned that evening carrying sandwiches and a smaller coat.

The boy met her at the door.

“Did you save it?”

“For now.”

He took the coat, running his fingers over the pockets.

Mara glanced down the corridor.

Then she sat on the stairs beside him and unwrapped the sandwiches.

“What would your name have been?” she asked."}
